articles.title: 'You will regret it': Angry resident confronts Democratic mayor during chaotic council meeting
articles.summary: Video captured a California immigration activist threatening to reveal Mayor Kevin McCarty's home address at a Sacramento City Council meeting after becoming angry with city policies.
articles.body: A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos Tuesday after an angry resident threatened the Democratic mayor's political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting officials to cut her microphone and temporarily recess the meeting. Video from Tuesday's city council livestream reviewed by Fox News Digital showed a woman confronting Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty during the public comment portion of the meeting, warning that protesters would continue disrupting city business if officials failed to address their concerns. "If you do not vote in our interest again, you will regret it," the woman said. "We protest. We stop things. We shut things down, Kevin. And careers." The woman then suggested that McCarty's political career had run its course. MEMPHIS CITY COUNCIL DEVOLVES INTO CHAOS AFTER DATA CENTER MORATORIUM VOTE POSTPONED "It's time for your f---ing career to end," she said, before raising the possibility of his retirement. As council officials repeatedly attempted to restore order, someone in the audience also urged the angry woman to show decorum. "F--- your decorum," she responded. The confrontation escalated further when the woman threatened to disclose the mayor's home address. "I do not give a f--- about your privacy," she shouted. "Do you want everyone to know your address? Because now I know your address." Her microphone appeared to be cut as she began reciting what she claimed was the mayor's address, and a council official warned her against disclosing private information. 'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING As shouting erupted in the council chambers, officials called a recess and council members left the dais. Approximately 20 minutes later, council members returned and resumed public comment. No audience members were removed, The Sacramento Bee reported. According to the newspaper, the confrontation with the woman, identified by the outlet as a local immigration activist, unfolded amid ongoing tensions over the city's immigration enforcement policies and its cooperation with federal authorities. Earlier in the meeting, McCarty announced that the council would postpone consideration of a $3.7 million Department of Homeland Security grant agreement amid questions about potential data-sharing provisions. Tuesday's incident marked the fifth time this year that Sacramento City Council members had recessed a meeting because of audience disruptions, according to The Sacramento Bee. The repeated confrontations have largely stemmed from activists' concerns about immigration enforcement and the city's sanctuary policies, the outlet reported. DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED' The mayor's office declined to comment on the incident to Fox News Digital. This week's outburst comes months after Fox News Digital reported that a live microphone captured McCarty and Vice Mayor Karina Talamantes discussing whether disruptive protesters could be barred from future council meetings. "We should go over this disruptions thing, because if we want to ban somebody in the future, like to take them out, we have to point out specifically," Talamantes was heard saying during the July meeting. "I know, but the city attorney said we can't do that," McCarty responded. The woman who confronted McCarty on Tuesday also appeared during the July meeting, when she shouted at the mayor, "Kevin, listen to me. Stop being an a--hole, dude. Listen to your f---ing constituents." Following the July incident, McCarty told Fox News Digital that council leaders were responsible for ensuring public meetings remained accessible and orderly. articles.title: Trump's massive DC triumphal arch project dealt another blow by federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge extended her order blocking construction of President Donald Trump's triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., putting the project on hold until at least Dec. 3.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington in Washington, D.C., was dealt another blow Wednesday when a federal judge extended an order blocking construction until at least early December. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her initial Nov. 5 temporary restraining order blocking construction of the arch for another 14 days, delaying progress on the structure until at least Dec. 3. The extension comes as Chutkan's original order was set to expire Thursday. The judge said the extension would give her additional time to consider lawsuits filed by the District of Columbia and Virginia seeking a longer-term injunction against the project. MULTIPLE KENNEDY FAMILY MEMBERS SEEK TO JOIN LEGAL BATTLE AGAINST TRUMP'S TRIUMPHAL ARCH The order marks the latest setback for one of the president's major projects in the nation's capital. Inspired by Paris' Arc de Triomphe, the proposed monument would stand near the Memorial Bridge, which connects Arlington National Cemetery to Washington, D.C. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the White House criticized the order, saying the project was being undercut by an "activist district court." "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added. EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE Chutkan issued the temporary restraining order earlier this month just hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project. The approval had cleared the way for construction to begin before the court intervened. Trump has previously said the triumphal arch would be converted into a military complex capable of rapidly deploying large numbers of drones, with snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition." The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. articles.title: Trump's China trip: Historic Xi-Putin talks, 'superintelligence' boast and other top moments
articles.summary: President Donald Trump declared the US the world leader in "superintelligence" at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, staking a tech claim amid the AI rivalry.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit featured an elaborate welcome, warm exchanges with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and a declaration of American technological dominance on Chinese soil. The gathering in Shenzhen culminated in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, with nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine among the issues on the table. Here are some of the standout moments from Trump's visit. XI BREAKS PROTOCOL TO PERSONALLY WELCOME TRUMP AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT AND MORE TOP HEADLINES Trump touts US 'superintelligence' on China's turf Trump declared the United States the world leader in "superintelligence" during remarks at the summit Thursday, making the assertion in one of China's major technology hubs. "The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution," Trump told APEC leaders. The remarks came as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors. Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic three-way talks Trump joined Xi and Putin for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia just after 3 a.m. ET, calling the gathering an opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons and address global conflicts. "As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth," Trump said. The president also said he had held extensive discussions with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine. "I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war." Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction. A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access. Xi rolls out red carpet for Trump Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome. The two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead. TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect." Trump strikes warm tone with Xi, Putin Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend." "President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it." Trump also told Xi, "You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship." "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it," he went on, telling the Chinese leader: "And I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem." During a separate encounter with Putin, Trump was heard saying, "Who is he? It's my friend. Nice to see you," according to video shared by Clash Report. articles.title: Manu Sánchez planta cara a Ayuso en RTVE y reivindica la historia de Andalucía: “Cuando fundamos Madrid, Cádiz ya tenía 2.000 años”
articles.standfirst: El humorista aprovechó su monólogo en 'El perro andaluz', de La 1, para contestar a las declaraciones de la presidenta madrileña sobre Andalucía
articles.summary: El humorista aprovechó su monólogo en 'El perro andaluz', de La 1, para contestar a las declaraciones de la presidenta madrileña sobre Andalucía
articles.body: Manu Sánchez ha aprovechado el monólogo de apertura de ‘El perro andaluz’, en La 1, para responder a Isabel Díaz Ayuso por sus declaraciones sobre Andalucía. La presidenta madrileña había criticado la etapa de los gobiernos socialistas y habló de una “red de gente garrapatera” que, según dijo, vivía del dinero público. Aunque después matizó que sus palabras se dirigían al socialismo y no a los andaluces, el humorista decidió contestarle. Sánchez anunció que le tocaba hacer de “maestro de Historia” y recurrió a los orígenes de la capital para reivindicar la antigüedad de las ciudades andaluzas. Recordó que Madrid surgió como una población fortificada de Al-Ándalus en el siglo IX y contrapuso esa fecha con la trayectoria de Cádiz, Sevilla, Córdoba y Granada. “Cuando fundamos Madrid, Cádiz ya tenía 2.000 años”, afirmó. También mencionó el teatro romano gaditano y la mezquita cordobesa. El presentador combinó las referencias históricas con críticas a los estereotipos que, a su juicio, todavía pesan sobre Andalucía. “Guarda tu condescendencia y complejo de superioridad con mi tierra”, llegó a decir, antes de insistir en que su intervención no iba dirigida contra los votantes del Partido Popular ni contra los ciudadanos de Madrid. Durante el monólogo también aludió a la gestión de Ayuso, a la polémica de las residencias durante la pandemia y a quienes deben abandonar sus comunidades para encontrar oportunidades laborales. Defendió que los territorios tengan recursos para que sus habitantes puedan desarrollar allí sus proyectos de vida. Sánchez cerró su intervención reivindicando la convivencia entre comunidades y mostró su afecto hacia la capital: “Viva Madrid, de corazón, de Madrid al cielo”. Después reservó la última frase para su tierra: “Y sobre todo, permítanme hoy, alto y libre, viva por siempre Andalucía”.

articles.title: 4 essential lessons we learned from the government’s dangerous war on ‘disinformation’
articles.summary: The White House once pressed platforms to curb speech; Trump's executive order reversed it, but new report warns oversight gaps could allow a repeat.
articles.body: In 2021, the White House issued a national strategy in which it asserted that "a crisis of disinformation and misinformation often channeled through social media platforms" was fueling "extreme polarization" that could lead to domestic terrorism. White House personnel sent messages to social media platforms suggesting their failure to remove or limit speech would lead to violence. Public scrutiny focused on these efforts when the Department of Homeland Security launched its short-lived Disinformation Governance Board in 2022. A newly released staff report from the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board ( PCLOB) examines this ill-informed campaign against "disinformation" on social media. In keeping with PCLOB’s mandate to ensure the federal government's efforts to prevent terrorism are balanced with the need to protect Americans’ privacy and civil liberties, the report evaluates the attempt to link disinformation to domestic terrorism and analyzes what policies were in place to prevent speech suppression. After a four-year investigation, PCLOB was provided no evidence to support the contention that disinformation fueled domestic terrorism. Nevertheless, former government actors encouraged social media companies to label questionable content as false, limit users’ ability to find it, and, in some cases, completely remove the content or the speakers’ accounts from their platforms altogether. CHRIS MURPHY CALLS FOR 'REGULATING THE INTERNET' SO PEOPLE WON'T FALL FOR A 'DEMAGOGUE LIKE DONALD TRUMP' In January 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to end this practice. But we are in danger of repeating the mistakes of this disturbing chapter if Americans fail to learn four key lessons from it. DAN GAINOR: WE GOT TWITTER/X AS A PLATFORM 20 YEARS AGO AND GLOBAL CENSORS STILL HATE AND FEAR IT First, speech suppression is an extreme response to perceived disinformation As PCLOB’s report explains, there is a range of government responses to disinformation that vary in their intrusiveness and civil liberties impact. Affirmative government speech is, and has historically been, a generally accepted and appropriate reaction to information the government considers to be wrong and dangerous. The government may state what it believes to be true and do so with the full authority it can bring to bear. But government efforts to encourage third-party social media platforms privately to "enforce their own terms of service" by removing or throttling speech with which the government does not agree are highly concerning. BIDEN'S 'ANTI-MAGA TASK FORCE' SPARKED INTERNAL ALARM ACROSS DOJ, NEW REPORT SHOWS Publicly available documents now confirm that government actors took steps to encourage social media platforms to suppress broad types of speech without considering whether the speaker was foreign or domestic, and without considering whether the speech was protected. They did not, for example, only target speech that constituted a "true threat" or incited what the Supreme Court calls "imminent lawless action." Compounding the civil liberties concerns, these government efforts to suppress speech largely occurred privately — often through direct communication between government officials and social media platforms. Were it not for lawsuits that forced discovery of these communications, the public likely never would have known the scope of the government’s involvement. FBI INVESTIGATED MOM OVER TIES TO ‘RIGHT-WING’ MOMS FOR LIBERTY GROUP, BOMBSHELL DOJ REPORT REVEALS Second, avoidance of explicit government coercion is insufficient to protect civil liberties Government lawyers responded to the lawsuits and the revelation of the (at best, unseemly) emails as they would be expected to do: by issuing guidance to ensure future communications were lawful. That primarily meant advising agencies and actors not to be "coercive." MACRON TRASHES AMERICAN FREE SPEECH AS RIOTS GRIP FRANCE — INTERNET UNLOADS: ‘ENORMOUS FOOL’ The clear thrust of many of these policies was that the executive branch believed that it was both appropriate — and in many instances advisable — for government actors to persuade social media companies to monitor or limit certain speech so long as the communications were framed as suggestions. It is of course questionable whether social media platforms would ever really find an email from the White House to be a suggestion, no matter how many disclaimers are appended to it. But even if they did, that does not make such communications good policy. The government may state what it believes to be true and do so with the full authority it can bring to bear. But government efforts to encourage third-party social media platforms privately to "enforce their own terms of service" by removing or throttling speech with which the government does not agree are highly concerning. UNEARTHED DOJ EMAILS EXPOSE TURMOIL OVER BIDEN-ERA MEMO URGING CRACKDOWN ON PARENTS And it would undoubtedly be terrible policy for the government to send to social media platforms secret lists of statements it believes to be wrong, accompanied by secret lists of accounts purveying these wrong statements. Whether such actions are lawful or not, the government should not be in the business of policing Americans’ speech. Third, efforts to counter foreign malign influence can quickly turn to countering disinformation more broadly The social media engagement practices that were utilized first to counter disinformation from malign foreign actors were, unfortunately, easily translated to countering domestic terrorism. The risk that the need to fight terrorism would be used to justify curtailing civil liberties is well recognized. Indeed, it is the reason that the 9/11 Commission recommended the creation of PCLOB. And it is why the commission recommended that "[t]he burden of proof for retaining a particular governmental power should be on the executive, to explain [both] that the power actually materially enhances security and that there is adequate supervision of the executive’s use of the powers to ensure protection of civil liberties. … If the power is granted, there must be adequate guidelines and oversight to properly confine its use." BRITAIN'S SWEEPING NEW CRACKDOWN ON 'ANTISOCIAL' BEHAVIOR SPARKS FREE SPEECH BACKLASH: 'PEAK INSANITY' Here, it was not at all clear that disinformation fueled domestic terrorism, or that it did so on any significant scale. Nor is it evident that government efforts to suppress such speech would enhance national security. Fourth, adequate policies and oversight do not currently exist to confine the government in any future efforts CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Trump’s executive order sets a clear direction against government efforts to pressure social media platforms to curtail speech. But prohibitions on attempts to suppress Americans’ lawful speech are not clearly stated in current agency policy and are not codified into law. That makes it relatively easy for the government to reverse course in the future and resume the types of counter-disinformation efforts described in PCLOB’s report. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Americans should not have to suspect — or fear — that the government is encouraging private companies to censor their speech. To effectively protect a nation, the government must perpetually prove itself worthy of trust.

Daisane's wife, Ayaan Aydid, 30, is present in the country illegally, a Trump administration official confirmed on Wednesday afternoon after an Alpha News report on the subject. Aydid crossed the U.S. southern border with Mexico in 2023, during former President Joe Biden's administration. SOMALI DAYCARE OWNER TIED TO FRAUD WINS MINNESOTA HOUSE RACE SPARKING ONLINE FURY: 'LOST STATE' After Daisane's victory, a video surfaced of Aydid detailing to the BBC how she crossed into the United States at the southern border, sparking questions about her immigration status. articles.title: Supreme Court urged to defang ‘criminal trap’ that has sent Trump officials to prison
articles.summary: Peter Navarro asks the Supreme Court to overturn his contempt of Congress convictions, arguing willfulness could make such prosecutions harder to prove.
articles.body: A Trump administration official who served four months in federal prison for defying a congressional subpoena is asking the Supreme Court to overturn his convictions in a case that could raise the bar for criminally prosecuting others who refuse to comply with Congress’s demands. Peter Navarro, who was a senior trade advisor to President Donald Trump during his first administration, filed a petition with the Supreme Court last month. Navarro currently serves in the Trump administration as senior counselor for trade and manufacturing. He was convicted in 2023 on two counts of contempt of Congress stemming from his refusal to provide testimony and documents to the Democratic-led House Jan. 6 committee on the grounds that he believed he was barred by executive privilege. If the justices take the case, they could make it harder to convict someone for defying a congressional subpoena by requiring proof that the person knew they were breaking the law. JUDGE TOSSES CASE AGAINST EX-FBI OFFICIALS ACCUSED OF LYING TO CONGRESS ABOUT HUNTER BIDEN INVESTIGATION Before Navarro’s trial, U. S. District Judge Amit Mehta ruled in August 2023 that he had failed to establish that Trump invoked executive privilege for the subpoena, barring him from relying on that claim as a defense. After serving his sentence, Navarro appealed his conviction to the U. S. Court of Appeals for the D. C. Circuit, which ruled that a person violates federal law by refusing to comply with a subpoena "even if he subjectively and mistakenly believed his default was lawful. " The three-judge panel ruled that only the president can invoke executive privilege under Article II, and Trump never granted Navarro protection. "Dr. Navarro claimed executive privilege before even seeing the subpoena and refused to turn over documents, appear for his deposition, or engage with the Select Committee’s efforts to accommodate his privilege claim," the court wrote. "A court, in other words, cannot simply take a defendant at his word that the President invoked privilege because doing so would impermissibly tangle separation-of-powers lines." But Abhishek Kambli, counsel for Navarro, argued the D.C. Circuit misinterpreted the statute, pointing to United States v. Murdock, a 1933 Supreme Court ruling that a taxpayer’s sincere but mistaken belief that the Constitution protected his refusal to answer investigators’ questions mattered in determining whether he acted "willfully." "We absolutely believe that we are correct on the law on this, because Congress chose to use the word willful when it put this statute together, and there's no reason to believe that willful applies any differently in this context than it has in just about every other one, but it would have the added effect of toning down lawfare and weaponization if we were to succeed," Kambli told Fox News Digital. The House voted to hold Navarro in contempt for failing to comply with a subpoena, but Kambli argued the Jan. 6 committee bypassed the negotiations traditionally used to resolve disputes involving executive branch officials. WHITE HOUSE LAWYER'S HARDBALL WARNING TO DEMS HAS LEGAL EXPERTS ON BOTH SIDES QUESTIONING ONE KEY THREAT "When it comes to executive branch officials, there was an accommodation process where they would negotiate terms of the appearance of the witness that's an executive branch official, and then determined whether executive privilege applies or not," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "What happened with the J-6 committee is that they short-circuited a lot of that and sent people straight to getting prosecuted and indicted." Kambli said a Supreme Court ruling in Navarro's favor could help "tone down the weaponization that could potentially occur" once Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. "What would happen is that if we were to win and the correct mental state is required to prove someone violated this law and get convicted and sent to jail, you would have fewer prosecutions for contempt of Congress because they're going to be much harder to prove," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "And what will happen is that there's less of an opportunity to wield a congressional subpoena in a weaponized manner rather than just through a legitimate legislative purpose, which Congress is limited to traditionally." Navarro’s lawyers filed the petition a week before Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called for investigating alleged Trump administration corruption, saying cases targeting those who "enabled" the president could send a "deterrence message" to young people considering administration jobs. Following Democrats’ wins in the 2026 midterm elections, lawmakers took to social media to vow investigations into Trump officials, with House Oversight Committee ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., posting on X, "LAWYER UP." However, Republicans still control both chambers of Congress until Democrats take control in January 2027. "We can't keep this up where people are utilizing law fare and other weaponization tactics to harm their political opponents, so we think that this petition would protect everyone in the long term and allow our politics to be better because we're not constantly trying to utilize congressional subpoenas as a way to indict people," Kambli told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Mike Davis, a conservative lawyer and founder and president of the Article III Project, which filed an amicus brief supporting the petition, said the Supreme Court must take this case up to end "lawfare." "Democrats weaponized Congress to throw Peter Navarro in prison for standing up for President Trump’s Executive privilege in good faith," Davis said. "The D.C. Circuit then ruled that good faith is no defense to contempt of Congress, and that turns every congressional subpoena into a criminal trap. It tears up more than two centuries of negotiation between the co-equal branches." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The petition from Navarro comes after the Supreme Court vacated the ruling against Steve Bannon. The former Trump White House strategist served four months in federal prison in 2024 after being convicted of two counts of contempt of Congress for defying a subpoena from the House Jan. 6 committee. In April 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s decision in his case and sent it back for further proceedings following the Justice Department's motion to dismiss his indictment.

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for rare three-way meeting in China
articles.summary: President Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin sat down for a rare meeting in China, with nuclear weapons and the Ukraine and Iran...
articles.body:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down for a meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday — a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.

All three made brief opening statements before meeting behind closed doors for about an hour and a half. The leaders did not offer joint or separate statements to reporters after the sit-down, and Mr. Trump immediately left for the airport to return home.

Before the gathering, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.

"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."

Cameras captured Mr. Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent entering a small conference room in Shenzhen to meet with Putin, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and other Russian officials.

As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."

Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."

Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being ethe main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

He said he intended to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.

Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is beleived to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.

Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .

China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."

"A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," Xi said, according to the Chinese news agency. "Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war."

A range of other global challenges are lingering in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.

The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.

Foreign conflicts loom large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island , which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."

And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported . Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

articles.title: Cruz says he and Talarico should sit down for coffee or tequila
articles.summary: Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) said he would be willing to work with Sen.-elect James Talarico (D), adding that he has invited Talarico for “a cup of coffee.” Cruz said he called Talarico on election night to congratulate him on his “impressive victory” and said, “I told him that night that I am happy to…
articles.body:
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) said he would be willing to work with Sen.-elect James Talarico (D), adding that he has invited Talarico for “a cup of coffee.”

Cruz said he called Talarico on election night to congratulate him on his “impressive victory” and said, “I told him that night that I am happy to work with him if he wants to work together on issues that matter and benefit Texas.”

“I invited him to come sit down, get a cup of coffee with me. We haven’t done so yet,” he said. “I might even give him a shot of tequila, see if he loosens up a little.”

In the midterm elections, Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country, turning the Lone Star State blue in a historic win. Alongside Talarico, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) to become the state’s first Latina governor.

The blue wave in Texas is in line with the rest of the country, where Democrats secured big wins in battleground states and flipped GOP-held seats in Kansas, South Carolina, Maine, Iowa, Alaska and Mississippi. The party took control of both chambers of Congress, holding 56 seats in the Senate.

Cruz previously called the midterm results “a blue tsunami” and “an a– kicking.”

He attributed the Republican Party’s huge losses to issues including the cost of living, the war in Iran and tariffs, expressing concerns about the future of Texas. “Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas,” he said.

Following his win, Talarico has said he would be willing to work with the Trump administration on issues surrounding immigration, economic relief and political reform.

“American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” Talarico said.

“It’s so much bigger than a party. We are tired of being pitted against each other. We’re tired of being told to hate each other. It’s been 10 years of this kind of politics,” he added.

articles.title: Results from Latino voters should make the GOP course correct, not despair
articles.summary: Wishful thinking that overstates the meaning of short-term shifts risks obscuring the unstoppable assimilation that is remaking Latino populations from within.
articles.body:
As the polls predicted , the decade-long movement of Latino voters toward the Republican Party came to an end on Nov. 3. That’s a big deal given that almost 15 percent of eligible voters in our closely divided nation are Latino. The fact that we are not currently deep into the second year of a Kamala Harris administration owes something to the 14 percentage point swing by Latinos toward the GOP in 2024.

But the exit polls indicate that from 2024 to 2026 , the Latino vote for Republicans declined from 46 to 33 percent and increased for Democrats from 51 to 65 percent. The historically low five percentage point Democratic advantage in the Harris-Trump race rebounded to a 32 percent margin in the midterms.

This is sure to tempt progressive pundits, activists and academics into believing that Latinos are supposedly coming home to the Democrats. After watching their “ demography as destiny ” dream collapse across the last half dozen election cycles, progressives are hungry for good news.

But a word to the wise: Wishful thinking that overstates the meaning of short-term shifts risks obscuring the unstoppable assimilation that is remaking Latino populations from within .

Understanding the Latino vote requires attention to two separate dimensions of change. Along the first are long-term shifts in partisanship that occur when any population moves toward the American mainstream. Along the second run, the day-to-day political dynamics that shape elections, particularly the economy but also the foreign and domestic policy issues prominent in any cycle.

The key point is that short-term fluctuations in the Latino vote, as we just saw, do not contradict the longer-term changes in the population’s political orientations. Quite the contrary, in fact. When Latinos in a specific election move toward the Democrats in response to issues that generally shape the American electorate, this is exactly what we would expect from a population becoming less distinct with each election cycle.

This November, Latinos were not voting for the Democrats as much as against a GOP that is associated with three toxic I’s: inflation, Iran and ICE — Immigration and Customs Enforcement. These issues are important to all Americans, although two characteristics of the contemporary Latino electorate are likely responsible for the shift this year.

First, the electorate is disproportionately young and working class . About 1 million Latinos turn 18 every year , so in these precarious times, it’s no surprise that 70 percent of Latinos prioritized the economy in 2024.

Second, the Latino electorate has a disproportionately large share of new voters with relatively weak partisan attachments , so it is less likely to stick with any party out of loyalty or habit.

Taken together, these two factors lead to a ruthless and retrospective Latino electoral calculus: Deliver economically or pack your bags. With Republicans in control of the White House and both chambers of Congress, it was clear to Latino voters who should be held accountable for the economic harm caused by inflationary tariffs, wars of choice and the deportation of non-criminal immigrants.

But these short-term factors are joined by a long-term dynamic: A Latino electorate that is socially and economically moving toward the mainstream . And as Latinos become more like other Americans, they will increasingly respond to the policy agenda that dominates the mainstream rather than acting as a distinct electorate. Given that the ideological middle in America remains the center right , this is bad news for Democrats.

In this, Latinos are traveling a well-worn path. A century ago, Italian , Polish and other European Catholic immigrants largely began their American political lives as Democrats. But over time, they assimilated and came to value the GOP’s message about economic prosperity and social mobility over ethnic group appeals. The Latino population is undergoing a similar transition .

As the midterms clearly showed, Republicans cannot make the Democratic mistake of taking Latino voters for granted. For starters, a population that continues to have strong immigrant roots creates challenges for a GOP that has been captured by its nativist wing. While many Latino American voters were amenable to Trump’s pitch on curtailing new immigrant arrivals, on Election Day they voiced their opposition to aggressive policies that deport long-established but unauthorized Latino immigrants.

If Republicans want to get back to building on their gains with a Latino electorate that was naturally moving in their direction just two years ago, they need to understand that Latino support comes with caveats . Policies that economically harm Latinos and target them for elevated policing and surveillance will give electoral opportunities to Democrats in any election year — 2026 being a perfect example — regardless of long-term trends.

The Democrats’ post-2024 course correction, which saw a focus on bread-and-butter economics and the reemergence of Blue Dog politics, stands as a lesson for Republicans. The task for the GOP is to take this electoral disaster as an opportunity for honest reflection, not for despairing about the Latino vote or doubling down on harmful domestic and foreign policies.

If a traditional Ronald Reagan-style conservatism reemerges in the GOP after the blue tsunami, reorienting the party toward economic prosperity and individual liberty, this will help the GOP regain lost Latino, and non-Latino, voters.

David L. Leal is a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution and a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin. Alvaro Corral is an assistant professor at The University of Texas – Rio Grande Valley.

articles.body:
It’s Thursday. Country musician Ella Langley — singer of the very popular “Choosin’ Texas” — swept at Wednesday night’s Country Music Association Awards, snagging wins for six of her nine nominations. When she accepted entertainer of the year at the end of the night, she told the crowd, “At this point, I’m sick of me.”

Programming note: We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

P resident Trump , Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin released a four-point “peace declaration” Thursday after holding a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China.

In a phone call after the meeting, the U.S. president said, “On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12. It went great…Fantastic relationships built.”

The agreement covers United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the threat of nuclear conflict, according to statements published by the three countries.

The leaders, who all hold permanent seats on the U.N. Security Council, said they are “committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges.” They also pledged to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

“We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet,” Trump told members of the press before the meeting became private.

Best buds: Trump referred to Putin as a “friend” as the leaders arrived for the trilateral chat.

“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, according to audio captured as he entered a room with Putin.

Trump, who has maintained a notably warm relationship with the Russian leader, held a separate bilateral meeting with Putin during his visit.

It’s the first time Trump and Putin have held one-on-one talks since their August 2025 meeting in Alaska, an attempt to advance negotiations toward ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

Reporters accompanying Trump had their phones confiscated Thursday as they prepared to leave the country.

“Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons,” a pool reporter wrote in a dispatch.

The move drew speculation about the administration’s reasoning.

Why? : Trump in a phone interview didn’t fully elaborate as to why. “Well, we want to be careful, and we didn’t want to have people have phones when they shouldn’t have phones, so we were very careful,” he said.

Speaking of Ella Langley … Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Wednesday blocked Trump’s judicial nominee T. Elliot Gaiser from being confirmed for a seat on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas because the nominee is not from Texas.

“I just refuse to be jammed by a non-Texan who has no trial experience, who hasn’t been vetted,” Cornyn told CNN . “And so, we provided the White House an alternative, and I’m hoping they take advantage of it because I don’t want the seat to go vacant either.”

Gaiser lived in Ohio before he was tapped to lead the Office of Legal Counsel at the Department of Justice. Trump formally sent Gaiser’s nomination on Monday.

A Cornyn aide told The Hill’s The Gavel that he instead pushed the White House for months to recommend Steve Fahey, a former federal prosecutor, for the vacancy.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, on Wednesday said Jim O’Neill, who served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, would not be considered to lead the National Science Foundation (NSF).

The rejection came hours after the White House withdrew its nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

Cassidy said O’Neill didn’t have the support to advance and that the vote had been canceled.

O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Cassidy said.

“His role in the firing of Dr. Susan Monarez raised further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF,” Cassidy continued. “Several of the committee members had those concerns.”

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” he added.

O’Neill does not have a science background. Prior to joining the Trump administration, he worked for venture capitalist Peter Thiel.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) says the GOP lost nine Senate seats in the midterms because they couldn’t control issues that affected voters most — the Iran war, gas prices and inflation.

“Any exit poll that you look at would tell you it was about the war, it was about the economy, it was about inflation, it was about gas prices. I think that’s what it came down to, none of which our candidates had much control over,” Thune told John Roberts , the anchor of Fox News’s “America Reports.”

Thune said that Trump’s decision to go to war poured cold water on the GOP’s chances, and independent voters shifted away from Republicans.

“We got to start delivering an economic message about the cost of living, the things the American people care about,” he added.

The average Thanksgiving dinner cost will be more expensive next week, per research from the American Farm Bureau Federation.

The cost for a 10-person dinner will increase to $5.86 per person, a 6 percent rise compared with 2025. It’s also the first annual increase in Thanksgiving dinner prices since 2022, when the average cost was $64.05, or $6.40 per person.

Prices spiked four years ago as inflation reached a 40-year high amid supply shocks and the first year of the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Iran war reaches your turkey: Farmers are facing higher prices overall: increased costs of fertilizer, labor expenses, rent and electricity bills.

And higher energy prices make filling your gas tank or snagging the already pricey flight even more expensive. AAA projected 73 million people will travel by car, while 5.96 million will take domestic flights this year.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) blamed Trump for high prices Thursday on the Senate floor.

“Everything is too damn expensive. It doesn’t matter what your favorite Thanksgiving dish is. The cost of everything on the Thanksgiving menu has skyrocketed because of Trump’s disastrous war, his costly tariff taxes and his idiotic trade war with Canada,” he said.

Tech mogul Elon Musk distanced himself from Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement Wednesday, saying he does not identify with the political movement despite his close ties to the president.

Musk told New York Times journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin that he is “not MAGA” and sought to explain that he does not necessarily align himself with the GOP’s positions.

“I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m like, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” Musk told Sorkin.

Not the brightest idea : Musk also said in the interview that his decision to spend $442 million on GOP candidates in the 2026 midterms, which saw a historic blue wave, left him feeling “ pretty foolish .”

Trump responded to Musk’s comments in an interview with NBC News . “MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well,” the president said.

articles.title: Flake knocks Musk campaign spending: ‘You probably ought to know what these candidates are standing for’
articles.summary: Former Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.) on Wednesday knocked Tesla CEO Elon Musk for his regret of spending more than $400 million on Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections, saying the tech leader “probably ought to know what these candidates are standing for.” CNN’s Erin Burnett played a clip of Musk’s comments during a virtual…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.) on Wednesday knocked Tesla CEO Elon Musk for his regret of spending more than $400 million on Republican candidates in the 2026 midterm elections, saying the tech leader “probably ought to know what these candidates are standing for.”

CNN’s Erin Burnett played a clip of Musk’s comments during a virtual interview with New York Times columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit, where the world’s richest person also said he was “ not MAGA ” and that he was not sure “what MAGA means.”

“He said, ‘I’m not MAGA if MAGA is blind adherence to a set of principles,'” Flake said. “MAGA is not blind adherence to a set of principles. It’s blind adherence to one individual. President Trump has said over and over, ‘I define what MAGA is.'”

“Before you put down a few hundred million dollars on an election, you probably ought to know what these candidates are standing for,” the former senator admonished.

Flake also noted that a “good chunk” of Musk’s campaign spending went to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who lost his bid for outgoing Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) seat to Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico (Texas). Musk poured $158 million into Texas PAC, a key super political action committee that backed Paxton.

The Arizona Republican said Paxton “had no business being a candidate were it not for President Trump propping him up.”

Musk told Sorkin on Wednesday that he felt “pretty foolish” for spending $442 million on GOP campaigns after Democrats made sweeping victories across the country.

He said what motivated him was having at least the House, the Senate or the White House be in Republican control going into 2029, but that he wanted neither party to hold a “supermajority.”

Musk also described himself as “ideologically quite moderate.”

The tech billionaire was a staunch supporter of Trump’s 2024 reelection campaign. He went on to lead the defunct Department of Government Efficiency following Trump’s return to the White House in 2025.

The two had a falling out in the months after, but they have been seen together on occasion since.

articles.title: Great advice from Glenn Beck: Play Grand Theft Auto 6 with your kids!
articles.summary: It’s nice to see that not all conservative thought leaders are reflexively negative on video games.
articles.body:
Unless you’ve been living under rock these past 24 hours, you know that the most anticipated video game of the year has just launched: Grand Theft Auto 6. It’s been 13 years since the last installment in this series, and people are dying to get their hands on it. In fact, some members of the military have even signed up for a special re-enlistment proposal that lets them have a four-day weekend to play the game if they agree to another two to six years of service.

Now, I’m more of a Nintendo guy, so I probably won’t get a copy, but I’m thrilled for the millions of people who will be enjoying the game. It looks great. Unfortunately, some politicians are out to rain on your parade.

This is nothing new, as plenty of political figures like to hate on video games , saying they’re violent or obscene. And yes, it’s true that Grand Theft Auto is named after a type of a crime, and lets you engage in morally reckless or outright evil behavior like robbery and murder. For Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), that’s a reason not to play it.

With all due respect, Congressman Burchett, you are dead wrong: Studies have shown there is no connection between violent video games and real-world violence. Shooting someone in a video game does not make you want to shoot someone in real life. If anything, video games probably have a positive social effect on the crime rate, because people who might be out committing crimes are playing video games instead.

You want young men to cause mayhem in society? Have them loitering about outside. You want them to leave you alone? Put Grand Theft Auto in their hands and send them into a basement somewhere. That’s the last you’ll see of those troublemakers.

Indeed, video games can be a form of socialization and bonding for young men, with each other and even with family members. That’s why I was glad to hear Glenn Beck, a conservative commentator, actually recommending that dads play the game with their sons.

Amen, Mr. Beck. I salute you for that. That’s much better advice for parents. Nice to see that not all conservative thought leaders are reflexively negative on video games. Grand Theft Auto 6 is a great potential bonding experience for young men and their friends, their brothers, their fathers and uncles and grandfathers. Don’t waste it, people! A game this good only comes around once every 13 years.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: No enemy required: Are all our systems really just this unreliable?
articles.summary: Recent widespread service disruptions at Microsoft, the FAA, and Chase Bank suggest that internal procedural failures during planned technical work pose a greater systemic risk than external cyberattacks.
articles.body:
In the span of five days, Americans lost access to some of the systems they depend on most. Microsoft 365 suffered an outage that disrupted email and collaboration tools for about a day . The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide after equipment on its telecommunications network became unstable. Three days later, Chase banking customers found themselves unable to move their own money .

So far, none of these events has been attributed to a cyberattack. Microsoft says it found no sign of one . Chase says its trouble was not cyber-related . The FAA says the evidence shows no indication of a cyberattack , and names a remote radio site where a contractor had been working as one of two potential sources while its investigation continues. Federal officials say they see no evidence that the outages are connected or that an adversary was behind them.

That should concern us far more than it seems to.

Over the last two decades, organizations have poured money into protecting their systems from hostile actors. We have built entire industries around cybersecurity. We run penetration tests, monitor hostile traffic, buy threat intelligence and employ teams whose sole purpose is keeping adversaries outside the perimeter. Those investments matter as the threats from the outside are real.

But by the organizations’ own accounts, at least two of these disruptions did not start outside the fence. They began during planned technical work. The danger may not have been a sophisticated attacker — it may have been merely a routine upgrade.

I spent 23 years in FAA air traffic control and retired as an air traffic manager. Since 2006, I have practiced and taught the FAA’s safety risk management process. I have watched organizations succeed because changes were evaluated before they went live. I have also watched them struggle when responsibility for a change became diffused and nobody owned the outcome.

Consider what has been disclosed. The FAA says a contractor had been working at a remote communications site, including deploying a new router , and that the site is one of two potential sources of the trouble. The root cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said an earlier network capacity upgrade caused trouble after a later system change , and its preliminary post-incident report describes a latent defect that left servers overwhelmed under load . By the company’s own account, planned work exposed a hidden flaw. It was not an attack.

Chase has attributed its outage to a software bug and has not said how the bug reached its systems.

That makes two of three incidents tied to planned work by their owners’ own accounts. I won’t speculate on the third.

A firewall can block hostile traffic. An intrusion detection system can flag suspicious activity. A security operations center can watch for adversaries around the clock. But none of those controls asks whether maintenance should happen in the middle of a Friday. None asks whether a rollback plan exists, whether a dependency was overlooked, or whether the people approving a change understand what happens if it fails. Those questions belong to management, not technology.

Aviation learned that lesson long ago. The agency’s latest safety management order took effect in September. Its requirement is plain: A planned change cannot proceed without a risk acceptance signature from a management official, and the decision is recorded in the agency’s risk register. Federal bank examiners have guidance of their own — a handbook that calls for a formal process for controlling and approving changes .

On paper, the process is simple, but a procedure on paper is not accountability in practice. The FAA has described the Nov. 13 router replacement as routine work of a kind done for decades without impact. I understand why. In my experience, though, “routine” might be the most dangerous word in any operation. Novel changes get scrutiny because everybody sees the risk. Routine changes get a nod because they worked the last hundred times. The hundred-and-first is the one that makes the front page of the newspapers.

I don’t know whether the router replacement was handled as a planned change under the FAA’s orders; the agency hasn’t said. The Washington Post reported on Nov. 17, citing a person close to the investigation, that an FAA official supervised the work, tested it and signed off shortly before the ground stop. If so, a signature exists. I still don’t know whether anyone accepted the risk before the work began, what assessment supported that decision or what testing was done against the live network. As members of Congress promise oversight on the ground stop, those are the questions to put to the FAA.

The same ones should be put to Microsoft and Chase: What changed? Who approved it? What testing did it pass before it touched a live system?

Those aren’t technical questions. They are leadership questions. Microsoft has released a preliminary post-incident report to its customers. The FAA and Chase should do the same, and all three should answer in language that customers, passengers and regulators can all understand.

More money will not fix this by itself. Neither will a new vendor, a new platform or a taller firewall. The next major disruption may not require an enemy at all. It may require nothing more than a work order and nobody clearly accountable for the result.

Vincent E. Bianco III is principal consultant of Marivin Consulting Services LLC and spent 23 years in FAA air traffic control, retiring as an air traffic manager.

articles.title: Chuck Todd says Democrats should ‘start with tariffs’ to lower cost of living
articles.summary: Former “Meet the Press” moderator and political pundit Chuck Todd said he expects the new, Democratic-led Congress to focus on lowering living costs, beginning with walking back the second Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs on foreign goods. “In the first hundred days, it’s about going after things this administration has done to raise the cost on…
articles.body:
Former “Meet the Press” moderator and political pundit Chuck Todd said he expects the new, Democratic-led Congress to focus on lowering living costs, beginning with walking back the second Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs on foreign goods.

“In the first hundred days, it’s about going after things this administration has done to raise the cost on the American public,” Todd told anchor Leland Vittert of NewsNation, The Hill’s partner network. “You start with tariffs. It’s sitting right there.”

“The Iran war is probably number two on the agenda in that its impact on people’s bottom line,” Todd added.

Democrats took back both chambers of Congress in a sweeping “blue wave” during November’s midterms, flipping GOP-held seats in key battlegrounds including Texas, Kansas, Maine and South Carolina on Election Day — and, more recently, in Mississippi and Alaska.

Prior to the elections, voters cited rising costs and the war in Iran under the first half of President Trump’s second term as top concerns impacting their choices at the polls. In a Reuters/Ipsos survey released the night before Election Day, 48 percent of respondents ranked affordability as the most important factor in deciding their vote.

In a Gallup survey , conducted last month, nearly half of those polled marked the economy as an “extremely important” factor in casting their ballots. In the poll, 47 percent said the same of the Iran war, while an additional 30 percent called the conflict “very important” to their election decisions.

Following the midterms, some Republicans admitted the Iran war and its associated economic impacts set the stage for the huge GOP losses, though the president has defended the conflict, instead blaming the blowout on candidate quality.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) pointed to cost of living as a “top issue” for voters, saying, “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high.”

“Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long,” Cruz added.

Vice President Vance also placed the blame for the GOP’s losses on the Iran war, saying, “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance said in a post.

During his interview with Vittert, Todd also warned Democrats to focus less on “retribution” against the executive branch and more on “operating the entire time in making government easier on people’s lives” — calls that came as the party tees up sweeping investigations into Trump administration officials.

“There are more effective ways to accomplish the larger goal of accountability on the executive branch, and at the same time, bringing down the cost for the American people,” he said.

articles.title: Peltola says Alaska voters did not elect her to be partisan
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) sent a signal Wednesday that she won’t be a partisan Democrat as a member of the Senate, saying voters did not elect her for partisanship. Peltola told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Alaskan voters were straightforward with a message of wanting help with “crippling” fuel, healthcare and necessities prices and…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) sent a signal Wednesday that she won’t be a partisan Democrat as a member of the Senate, saying voters did not elect her for partisanship.

Peltola told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Alaskan voters were straightforward with a message of wanting help with “crippling” fuel, healthcare and necessities prices and that the voters’ support did not come because of a desire for partisanship from the senator-elect.

The Hill’s partners at Decision Desk HQ projected late Tuesday that Peltola, 53, would win the Alaska Senate race over incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

Peltola’s win means Democrats have netted a total of nine Senate seats, creating a 56-seat majority in the Senate for the party.

Peltola is a former congresswoman from Alaska and will be the first native-born Alaskan to serve in the U.S. Senate.

The Alaska Democrat’s victory was an upset in a state that commonly leans toward the GOP. But Republicans faced an uphill battle in this year’s midterms, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down.

Sullivan and the GOP have also complained about the existence of a second Dan Sullivan in the race who ran as an independent. Peltola has denied reporting that her campaign was involved with the second Sullivan running for the Senate.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola said in a post on the social platform X late Tuesday.

“Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work,” she added.

The nine Senate seats that Democrats have flipped is the most in nearly seven decades. The last time Democrats notched nine or more Senate seats in a midterm former President Eisenhower was in the White House, per the AP.

articles.title: Sasse to release memoir on his life, family amid cancer battle
articles.summary: Former Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.) announced Thursday he will release a new memoir reflecting on his life and the passage of time next year, which he penned alongside his daughter amid his battle with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer. “Fighting cancer is… uh…not as fun as you might expect, but…working on a book with your kid…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.) announced Thursday he will release a new memoir reflecting on his life and the passage of time next year, which he penned alongside his daughter amid his battle with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer.

“Fighting cancer is… uh…not as fun as you might expect, but…working on a book with your kid is pretty great. Over the past few months, my daughter Alex and I wrote a book in hospital hallways,” Sasse wrote Thursday on social platform X. “It’s not a cancer memoir (woof that’s boring) — but some of our reflections on time, habits, workaholism, and family.”

The book, “Redeem the Time: The Strange Gift of Dying and the Lost Art of Living,” is set to be published in March. The former senator’s announcement came almost a year after he was diagnosed with cancer and told he had just months to live.

“We’re all on the clock, and although death is absolutely wicked, the strange ‘ gift of dying ‘ is that it shatters our self-delusions about control,” he added in the social media post.

Sasse has been public about his cancer battle, opening up to The New York Times about his diagnosis in an interview earlier this year. During the conversation, published in April, he praised his doctors at MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and said, despite his cancer having spread, he felt less pain than he did before.

At the time, the former lawmaker told the Times the idea of leaving behind his kids was taking a toll on him.

“I didn’t like the idea of my 14-year-old son not having a dad around at 16,” Sasse said in the interview. “I didn’t like the idea of my daughters, who are 22 and 24, not having their dad there to walk them down the aisle. I felt a real heaviness about that.”

In a phone interview with Axios on Thursday, Sasse credited his daughter Alex with half of the idea for the book.

“[She] pushed me to do this as a joint project with her. So that was half of it,” Sasse told Axios. “The other half is I’m not dead yet. So why not try to do something to be of use and love to your neighbor and try to serve somebody?”

The former Nebraska senator left the upper chamber in 2023 to become president of the University of Florida, but he resigned the following year after his wife, Melissa, was diagnosed with epilepsy.

In the Axios interview, Sasse said the concept of being rich with time was a central theme of the book.

“We’re not just the materially richest people at any time and place in history, but we’re also the time-richest people,” Sasse told Axios. “And yet, we seem pretty dang miserable. Which is weird, because we ought to be able to make conscious choices about how to invest or redeem the time.”

articles.title: Trump brushes off Musk distancing from MAGA
articles.summary: President Trump brushed off comments from tech titan Elon Musk that he isn’t part of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement and that he felt “pretty foolish” for the hundreds of millions of dollars he spent backing Republicans in the midterms. “He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News in a phone call…
articles.body:
President Trump brushed off comments from tech titan Elon Musk that he isn’t part of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement and that he felt “pretty foolish” for the hundreds of millions of dollars he spent backing Republicans in the midterms.

“He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News in a phone call Thursday while flying back from Asia. “What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask — there are lots of definitions out there.”

“MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well,” he continued. “But Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”

Musk, speaking remotely to The New York Times’s Andrew Ross Sorkin at the annual DealBook Summit on Wednesday, said he is “not MAGA.”

He added, “At least I’m not like — I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m like, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

“I think there are positives and negatives in both parties,” he said.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent a whopping $442 million on Republican campaigns for this year’s midterms. Ultimately, Democrats won both the House and the Senate.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money. Obviously, you can put a lot of money into an election and have an effect that is relatively minor, and I think that was the case here.”

Trump and Musk have had a very public on-again, off-again relationship.

Musk had a history of criticizing Trump, but then backed him during the 2024 presidential campaign, pumping nearly $300 million into Trump’s and other Republicans’ campaigns.

Trump put him in charge of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a new office created by the administration to cut government spending.

The tech billionaire left DOGE in 2025, and the two had a brief falling out, but they have since become closer again. He traveled with Trump for the president’s trip this week to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

articles.title: Senate Republicans reject war powers resolution to end Iran conflict
articles.summary: Senate Republicans on Wednesday blocked a measure that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities in Iran. It’s not the first time such a measure has come up for a vote in the Senate this year, but Democrats hoped for success after a midterm election that saw many voters support Democrats out of opposition…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans on Wednesday blocked a measure that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities in Iran .

It’s not the first time such a measure has come up for a vote in the Senate this year, but Democrats hoped for success after a midterm election that saw many voters support Democrats out of opposition to the conflict.

The vote failed 48-51. GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.), who have voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war, joined almost the entire Democratic caucus.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel, was the only Democrat to vote against it. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted for the resolution in September, voted against the current version.

“I’ve supported some. I mean, you do know resolutions differ from each one. This one doesn’t go to the president, so it’s just a statement from Congress,” Tillis told reporters. “I’ve made that statement. I don’t need to vote on a Democrat resolution to make that statement.”

The measure, known as a war powers resolution, is mostly a signaling vote. Democrats wanted to put Republicans on the record voting against ending the war , even though if the resolution had passed, Trump likely would not have signed it.

Thursday’s vote was the first time either chamber voted on the war powers resolution since the November midterms .

The House passed a complementary resolution in mid-September, led by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), by a vote of 220-204. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in that case to limit Trump’s military actions against Iran.

The Senate war powers vote comes as the cost of the conflict has gone up since October, when it was just more than $47 billion.

Arthur Miller, the deputy comptroller for budget and appropriations affairs at the Pentagon, told Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on Thursday the updated cost of the Iran war was $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13.

The figure includes munitions costs, equipment replacement costs and operational costs, but does not include the totality of damage to U.S. military facilities in the Middle East.

articles.title: DOJ, DHS launch hub to fight cyber crime
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a new hub to combat online cyber crime Wednesday, specifically targeting criminal scams and sextortion schemes. The launch comes amid growing concern after a series of tech outages in recent days, though the government has insisted there is no indication cyberattacks were…
articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a new hub to combat online cyber crime Wednesday, specifically targeting criminal scams and sextortion schemes.

The launch comes amid growing concern after a series of tech outages in recent days, though the government has insisted there is no indication cyberattacks were responsible.

More than 30 federal agencies along with hundreds of state and local partners are part of the initiative, which will connect public and private entities to help stop cyber criminals.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible. It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support,” the DOJ said in a statement.

The government will also use AI-powered tools through a private partner, TRM Labs, the DOJ said.

President Trump previously ordered multiple federal departments and agencies to create the center to combat cyber crime in a March executive order .

“Cybercrime, fraud, and predatory schemes are draining American families of their life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work, and destroying the lives of our youth,” he wrote in the order.

Cyber crime and sextortion schemes have become a growing concern, especially amid the rise of AI. The FBI said last week that North Korean hackers had stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months. And some recent hacks have even occurred without human involvement; top AI companies publicly identified instances of their unreleased models escaping and hacking other companies.

The AI boom and accompanying cyber crime has already been a focus for lawmakers in Washington. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), with the support of first lady Melania Trump, co-sponsored the Take It Down Act, a law that criminalized the publication of sexually explicit deepfake images online. The law, signed in 2025, recorded its first conviction in April.

Trump administration officials participated in the annual worldwide threats hearing Wednesday on Capitol Hill, where the recent outages involving U.S. air traffic, financial institutions and even the National Security Agency (NSA) were top of mind for lawmakers.
